newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest flood concerns may cut hydropower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest flood concerns may cut hydropower.

text.p: Flows through the 6,150 megawatt (MW) Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River in Washington State are being cut back to minimize the threat of downstream flooding, a spokeswoman for Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) said Tuesday.
Out-flow from Grand Coulee will be targeted at 140,000 cubic feet per second (cfs), down 22 percent from recent levels of 180,000 cfs, Crystal Ball at BPA said.
But officials at Grand Coulee, which is operated by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, said an exact plan for operations had not yet been determined.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has requested that flows from Bonneville Dam, the last hydropower project on the Columbia, be limited to 440,000 cfs due to increased concerns of flooding near Portland, Oregon.
In order to limit out-flow at Bonneville, Grand Coulee--the uppermost U.S. project on the Columbia--will operate below capacity until conditions change, Ball said.
Flood worries have grown amid this week's warmer weather and increased snowmelt, which has swollen streamflows into regional hydropower projects.
Flows at Chief Joseph Dam on the Columbia were forecast at 175,000 to 180,000 cfs through the end of the week, well above maximum generating capacity.
The runoff surge comes as required spill began Monday night at Lower Columbia River dams.
BPA does not anticipate any problems meeting the spill requirements, and will maintain its strategy of minimizing excess spill, which can be harmful to migrating fish.
"We are trying to maximize power generation to minimize spill," the BPA spokeswoman said.
Aside from the five power turbines planned to be idle over the spring runoff season, three small turbines remained off-line as of Tuesday, according to BPA.
The units were a 99 MW turbine at The Dalles due back April 24; a 60 MW unit at Bonneville due back May 1; and an 80 MW turbine at McNary due back May 8, Ball said.
